Comparison Test: Audi SQ5 vs. BMW X3 vs. Genesis GV70 vs. Mercedes-AMG GLC

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3142 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Caranddriver

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From the November/December 2026 matter of Car and Driver.
  • It has been revealed that the vehicles assembled here are not the starring members of their makers’ lineups.
  • We could have made a wider casting call for this production, but to ensure that the chosen crossovers weren’t forgettable, we opted for the more muscular variants, the ones with a more potent optional engine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From the November/December 2026 matter of Car and Driver.

It has been revealed that the vehicles assembled here are not the starring members of their makers’ lineups. They aren’t built for lapping racetracks, crossing the Rubicon Trail, or carrying a crew of seven. Instead, compact luxury crossover SUVs, as their compound-modifier designation suggests, play multiple roles. As premium-brand offerings, there’s an expectation of luxury. As four-door utilities, they must accommodate passengers and cargo. And as the more sporting examples of their ilk, they should exhibit a degree of athleticism. Living at the intersection of a variety of vehicle types, they need to demonstrate versatility and range, rather than excel with a singular ability.

We could have made a wider casting call for this production, but to ensure that the chosen crossovers weren’t forgettable, we opted for the more muscular variants, the ones with a more potent optional engine. That dramatically narrowed the field of candidates.

See all results for new 2026 Audi SQ5 for sale near 32830.

The Audi Q5 is a relatively fresh face, having just been redesigned for the 2025 model year. The SQ5 is the model that fit our bill, with its 362-hp turbocharged 3.0-liter V-6, seven-speed dual-clutch automatic, and sport-tuned adaptive air-spring suspension. The Prestige package ($5900) and Black Optic package ($1900) were the chief items pushing this crossover’s $66,795 base price to $76,370.

It has been revealed that the BMW X3 is a seasoned player in this arena, and the M50 xDrive best met our criteria. The turbocharged 3.0-liter inline-six has bulked up and boasts 393 horsepower and a robust 428 pound-feet of torque. It’s paired with an eight-speed automatic, adaptive M suspension, M Sport brakes, and an M Sport rear differential. To the BMW’s $67,850 base price, our test example added a modest load of options, which included the Premium package ($2750) and the M Sport Professional package ($600). The result was the lowest as-tested price, at $72,050.

It has been revealed that where you find a BMW, you typically find a Mercedes. Here, that’s the GLC in its newly introduced-for-2027 AMG GLC53 guise. It brings an enhanced supercharged and turbocharged 3.0-liter inline-six that makes 443 horsepower, a nine-speed automatic, AMG Ride Control suspension with adaptive damping, and rear-axle steering. Its $71,350 base price soared to $85,920, inflated by extras that included the Pinnacle trim ($3900), the AMG Dynamic Plus package ($2000), and the Driver Assistance package ($1950).

The award-winning Genesis GV70, with multiple 10Best trophies on its mantel, was a natural to include. It arrives in 3.5T guise, powered by a 375-hp twin-turbocharged 3.5-liter V-6 paired with an eight-speed automatic. It surprised us by having the highest base price, at $72,045, but in Prestige Graphite trim, there was little more to add, resulting in an as-tested figure of $73,895.

See all results for new 2026 Audi SQ5 for sale near 32830.

What about the many other hopefuls from Alfa Romeo, Cadillac, Lexus, Lincoln, Land Rover, and Volvo? Most were screened out due to insufficient horsepower below our 350-pony threshold, while dedicated hybrids and electrics were not invited. Casting is a cruel process.

Recent findings suggest that let’s face it; none of this quartet have movie-star looks. The GV70, though most familiar (the design dates from 2022), is still pleasing to our eyes. The GLC’s appearance doesn’t break much fresh ground, but its long hood and rakishly set-back greenhouse give it an aristocratic vibe. The Audi’s fresh sheetmetal somehow seems not so fresh, and also not so interesting; it was the hardest of the four to pick out in traffic. Then there’s the BMW. Like a celebrity who experiments with creative facial hair or a weird ’do, BMW periodically feels the need to challenge its fans by changing up its look. Unfortunately, that’s where the X3’s design now finds itself.

Industry observers note that HIGHS: Comfortable seats, capable chassis, solid feature content. LOWS: Forgettable looks, cramped rear quarters, not really a standout anywhere. VERDICT: Plenty of ability but eschews the spotlight.

That change-for-change’s-sake mantra reaches full flower in the X3’s interior. The operation of the outboard air vents and the placement of their controls are just annoying, as are the haptic door-lock buttons. “What the hell is going on with the door panels?” asked associate news editor Jack Fitzgerald. The design aims to be more futuristic than luxurious, but BMW’s vision of tomorrow is somewhat dystopian. “There’s nothing I like about these design choices,” said managing testing editor David Beard, “not one thing.” Screens and lighting set the scene, the better to distract you from the cheap-looking materials. After dark, though, the offending bits recede, and the glowing mood lighting enhances the atmosphere. Space is not an concern. The back seat comfortably accommodates two, but the shape of the seatback makes it uncomfortable for three (although that’s probably a rare use case for this segment). Up front, some of us found the driver’s seat to be narrow, but it’s highly effective at holding you in place during cornering.

Look at the SQ5’s dash, and it’s more like an assemblage of screens than a coherent design—the tacked-on passenger’s display is part of the Prestige package. Our car’s red seats and suede door panels were enlivening elements, but the patterned black plastic trim would look downmarket even in an A3. The driver’s chair was deemed good for a variety of body types, and the adjustable-height center armrest ups the comfort quotient. The SQ5 was also one of two vehicles in this test with seat massagers (the Genesis was the other). Its back seat, though, was the hardest to access and the least comfortable once you fold yourself into place—a consequence of the SQ5’s shortest-in-test wheelbase.

The GLC53’s cabin looks richer than its German compatriots’, and this is one Mercedes model whose massive screen isn’t larger than life. Whereas BMW tries pointlessly to reinvent the air vent, Mercedes shows what a quality execution looks like. This AMG steering wheel still has annoying touch-swipe pads, though. We also noticed that the bloated center console impinges on the driver’s kneeroom, and the inductive charging pad buried deep within made the Mercedes the car in which you’re most likely to leave your phone (it will warn you that you’ve left it inside). Finally, the GLC’s set-back cabin results in a smaller cargo hold than others here.

HIGHS: Lowest as-tested price, best fuel economy, just misses first place in most measures of performance. LOWS: Odd-duck appearance, off-putting interior, not so richly equipped. VERDICT: An SUV that dares you to like it.

Recent findings suggest that the GV70’s interior is the most glam, even more so than the Mercedes’s. “Easily the nicest,” Beard said. “You notice it from the moment you sit down.” Partial credit goes to the nonboring color scheme—blue with splashes of bright red—but don’t discount the glossy carbon-fiber-weave trim, the bright stainless-steel finishes, the ovoid shapes, and the quality-feeling switchgear. We love the rotary controller for the infotainment, which feels like quality. Unfortunately, it also feels like, and is located just ahead of, the rotary shifter. That quibble aside, the user-friendly GV70 took top marks in ergonomics. The Genesis also boasts comfortable, though firm, front chairs, with bonus points for their extendable under-thigh support.

If it’s an action hero you’re seeking, look first to the Mercedes. It has the strongest résumé, with not just the most horsepower but also the most torque, at 443 pound-feet (472 with a 10-second overboost function), just shading the BMW. Though tasked with carrying the greatest mass (4669 pounds), the boosted inline-six shrugs that off, and the AMG races to 60 mph in a launch-controlled 3.7 seconds, or in 4.7 seconds from a rolling 5-mph street start. Both of these results are best in test. So, too, are the quarter-mile time of 12.2 seconds at 113 mph and, thanks to the optional AMG Dynamic Plus package, the top speed of 167 mph, should you have to outrun a hail of bullets from machine-gun-wielding bad guys. All of this was plenty evident from behind the wheel, where the Mercedes felt like it wanted to storm the autobahn.

Sources indicate that the BMW, with its “fantastic powertrain” (Beard again), was just a beat behind. Commendably boasting the lowest curb weight of 4474 pounds, the X3 posted a 60-mph time of 4.0 seconds flat, with a street-start figure of 4.9 seconds, both second best among our foursome, as was its quarter-mile time. Exhaling through quad exhaust outlets, and piping the exhaust note through the audio system, the vocal straight-six sounds great when giving its all. “The grunt is always right there,” noted Buyer’s Guide associate editor Andrew Wendler, but if you somehow don’t trust the highly responsive transmission to deliver—or you just want a more theatrical experience—you can pull and hold the downshift paddle to trigger a 10-second Sport Boost mode. It puts the powertrain into its max-sport settings, although it had no measurable effect at the test track. It does call up a cool 10-second countdown graphic in the instrument cluster. “It reminded me of the Power Rangers activating,” Wendler said.

According to recent reports, the Audi also has a potent powertrain that’s always ready to break into a run, although it doesn’t sound quite as good as the others when doing so. “The 90-degree V-6 doesn’t have much character,” opined Beard. Nevertheless, with 406 pound-feet of torque, the SQ5 scampers to 60 mph in 4.3 seconds, or 5.2 seconds from a rolling start. Its seven-speed was the only dual-clutch automatic here and had the expected snappy responses but almost none of the low-speed lurching behavior commonly found in such transmissions.

HIGHS: Bucks-up cabin that’s a pleasure to interact with, blissful ride, quiet cruising.LOWS: Slowest of the group, trails on the skidpad, eyebrow-raising base price.VERDICT: Not the hardest-charging but still undeniably endearing.

According to recent reports, with the second-smallest stable of ponies at 375, along with a lowest-in-test 391 pound-feet of torque, the Genesis had noticeably less vigor than the Germans. That bore out at the track, where the GV70’s 60-mph time of 5.1 seconds was 0.8 second behind its nearest rival. The GV70 tied the Audi in 30-to-50-mph passing but otherwise brought up the rear in all acceleration tests. Still, the Genesis is hardly slow, and the V-6 makes the right noises when the virtual tach needle climbs. For the most part, fuel economy represents a bit part for these players, but the BMW’s 28 mpg in our hands bested the rest of the group and shaded the second-place Audi by 4 mpg. Meanwhile, the Genesis racked up the biggest bar tab, quaffing premium at a rate of 21 mpg.

Asked to show their softer side, the Mercedes and the BMW struggle. They remain firm even in the mellowest suspension modes, and any leftover compliance goes away if you switch into Sport. Of the BMW, Fitzgerald noted, “The suspension really beats you up on this loop, especially in Sport.” The X3 suffered noticeable head toss on the more challenging secondary roads.

Driven over rumble strips or expansion joints, the SQ5 seemed a shade less solid than the others. We posited that it was the lightest car here; actually, the Audi is second to the BMW but only by 16 pounds.

HIGHS: Pavement-searing acceleration, faithful steering, loads of stick. LOWS: Stiff ride, tiresome road noise, budget-busting price. VERDICT: A hugely talented but sometimes annoying A-lister.

None of the Germans rode as well as the Genesis, which barely acknowledged broken pavement. Wendler praised it as “serene on the highway.” Furthering that impression, the GV70 was also the quietest by far, registering just 19 sones at 70 mph.

On the handling loop, the flip side for the GV70 was a bit more body lean in aggressive cornering, though that’s a trade-off many owners would be happy to make. Shod with Michelin Primacy Tour A/S tires, the GV70 didn’t have the grip of the other cars. It also turned in the longest stopping distance, although its firm pedal feel won plaudits, as did the SQ5’s.

Sources indicate that the Audi hangs on in the corners—like the Mercedes, it wears Michelin Pilot Sport 4 SUV tires—but the steering doesn’t have much to say. We didn’t love the BMW’s steering either, but its handling chops are substantial even if its Pirelli P Zero All Season footwear placed it third in skid-pad grip with 0.85 g (a previous X3 M50 wearing Goodyear Eagle F1 summer rubber did 0.90 g). With four-wheel steering, the GLC53 turns in eagerly, and we also liked the distinct on-center accuracy. Furthermore, it turned in the best skid-pad numbers and shortest stopping distance.

Coolly capable though it may be, the BMW was hard to warm up to. It hit a lot of marks, and not just at the test track. Its potent powertrain also had the best fuel economy. The Bimmer had the lowest as-tested price, but the least money bought the least equipment, and no one was a fan of the interior—the design, the materials, or interacting with it.

It has been revealed that the Audi had no glaring weaknesses—unless you were trying to climb into the back seat—but no scene-stealing moments either. The powertrain and the chassis are undeniably accomplished, but the SQ5 would shine brighter if Audi could recapture some of its design magic, both inside and out.

According to recent reports, in this high-strung company, the Genesis was decidedly not the sportiest, but it should be sporty enough for most drivers. It’s easily the most comfortable, arguably the most luxurious, and just so pleasant to interact with. That was enough for second best overall, despite a last-place finish in most performance metrics.

Recent findings suggest that the Mercedes ultimately stole the show after acing our track tests. The GLC53 was engaging and exciting. “This is a machine doing powerful stuff, and you’re part of it,” Wendler noted. While we admired the SUV’s abilities, it was not free of irritants, with road noise, ride quality, and some ergonomic foibles trying our patience. Sharp-eyed accountants might also point out that the as-tested price was much higher than the others, but some $5K of that was costume jewelry such as black leather with red stitching, 21-inch AMG cross-spoke wheels, and the AMG Night package. All of those options could easily be shed without dimming the GLC53’s star power. And then there’s this truism: Great talent rarely comes cheap.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Off The AppStore, a weekly feature with a twist. Namely, while these - as with all the games we cover here - are games that you can play on your phone, they're ones that operate outside of the realms of the major two ways to play: The Google Play Store and the Apple AppStore.

That means that there might be a bit of work required in downloading alternative AppStores or  APKs, or that the games can simply be played in your phone browser. We'll make sure to detail that for each game, though. Anyway, read on to find a new game or experience to play Off The AppStore.

Things are never as scary as they seem until we're alone. There's nothing scarier than what our own minds can conjure from the dark depths of reality and fantasy. Even in our own homes, we can feel totally vulnerable and exposed when it comes to dealing with entities unbound by the laws we've come to follow and believe. Even something as simple as a rainy day can seem haunting when we don't know what to expect. This is what Sulpiride is trying to show us with Dremor, and now we have to experience the fear of being alone and someone out there knowing that we're alone.

You find yourself heading home after a long day of work, living alone in a small apartment, and trying to have a peaceful evening. You've got some leftovers and your own space, albeit marred by shoddy wiring that can take out all your electricity if a moth flaps a little too hard. It's a simple and quiet life that you've got, but you can't shake the feeling that something's wrong. The building isn't just old; it feels disturbingly devoid of life. But you know that there have to be neighbours, because all those sounds have to be coming from somewhere.

Recent findings suggest that after the electricity goes out and a wave of sleep washes over you, you must find your way through the darkness to try and have a nice night's sleep. The next day begins, and the rain greets you with some enthusiastic pats that thankfully aren't breaking through the wood, at least for now. You boot up your reliable old computer to check your emails and see that the rain has actually shut down part of the city, which means that you get to stay home! This nice surprise is accompanied by reports of increased disappearances and mysterious messages from someone demanding you come to them OR ELSE.

It has been revealed that dremor is a 3D first-person PS1-style horror story where you have no idea what's going on or why you've been targeted. It takes time to build things up and traps you in a seemingly normal life that's more uncomfortable than you realise. At this point, all you can hope to do is be on your guard, make it through the night, and sleep to dremor.

Dremor is available to download and play from its itch.io page!

Scientists discover that leukemia can begin developing 50 years before diagnosis

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1580 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A deadly form of blood cancer may begin taking shape more than 50 years before a person is diagnosed, according to new research revealing the surprisingly long and predictable path to leukemia.
  • According to recent reports, scientists have reconstructed how acute myeloid leukemia (AML) develops over a lifetime, discovering that in two-thirds of the cases studied, the first genetic mutation that helped drive the cancer appeared before age 20.
  • It has been revealed that the findings suggest that doctors may one day be able to identify people at risk of developing leukemia years or even decades before symptoms appear.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A deadly form of blood cancer may begin taking shape more than 50 years before a person is diagnosed, according to new research revealing the surprisingly long and predictable path to leukemia.

According to recent reports, scientists have reconstructed how acute myeloid leukemia (AML) develops over a lifetime, discovering that in two-thirds of the cases studied, the first genetic mutation that helped drive the cancer appeared before age 20. These early changes could remain largely unnoticed for decades before eventually contributing to the disease.

It has been revealed that the findings suggest that doctors may one day be able to identify people at risk of developing leukemia years or even decades before symptoms appear. They also raise the possibility of preventing the cancer by slowing the growth of abnormal blood cells long before the disease takes hold.

Blood Samples Reveal Leukemia's Hidden History.

Published in Nature, the study was conducted by researchers at the University of Cambridge and University College London (UCL). By examining blood samples collected over many years, including some obtained as long as 15 years before diagnosis, the team pieced together a detailed history of how leukemia develops.

According to recent reports, the scientists treated these stored samples as a kind of genetic fossil record. Using highly sensitive DNA sequencing and mathematical models, they worked backward to estimate when cancer-related mutations first appeared, how swiftly the affected cells multiplied, and how they competed with other blood cells as the disease approached.

AML is an aggressive blood cancer that affects approximately 2,700 people in the UK annually. Its outlook is often poor, with only about one in six patients surviving at least five years after diagnosis.

Scientists have long known that many otherwise healthy older adults carry blood cells with mutations associated with leukemia. This condition, called clonal hematopoiesis, does not necessarily lead to cancer. In fact, most people with these mutations never develop AML. Until now, researchers have struggled to understand why some individuals progress to leukemia while others do not, partly because they lacked a detailed record of the genetic changes occurring in the years before diagnosis.

To investigate, the team turned to samples from the UK Collaborative Trial of Ovarian Cancer Screening (UKCTOCS). That project involved approximately 50,000 women who provided blood samples annually for as long as 11 years.

Recent findings suggest that for the upcoming analysis, researchers examined samples from 47 women who eventually developed AML, with an average age at diagnosis of 72. They compared these findings with samples from 46 similar women who remained free of blood cancer.

Cancer Mutations Can Remain Hidden for Decades.

The results revealed an extraordinary timeline. In two-thirds of the women who developed AML, the earliest mutation contributing to the disease was estimated to have occurred before their 20th birthday.

At first, the altered blood cells multiplied extremely slowly, sometimes taking several years just to double in number. But as additional cancer-driving mutations accumulated, their growth accelerated dramatically.

Sources indicate that each fresh mutation typically increased the rate of growth by roughly two to three times. By the time cells had acquired four mutations capable of driving cancer, their populations could double within weeks instead of years.

Perhaps even more surprising was how consistently these populations behaved.

Industry observers note that researchers found that groups of genetically related blood cells, known as clones, generally expanded at predictable rates once they became established. Their growth tended to slow only when they faced limited space or competition from another clone that was multiplying more swiftly.

Industry observers note that this consistency could have vital medical implications. By measuring the growth of a particular clone using just a few blood samples, scientists may be able to estimate how large that population will become many years into the future, potentially even decades later.

A Hidden Warning Sign of Leukemia.

The researchers also identified a striking pattern that appeared in some patients well before leukemia was diagnosed.

Industry observers note that in at least one-third of AML cases, a single population of mutated blood cells had grown so extensively that it dominated the blood years before diagnosis. Scientists call this process a "somatic sweep.".

None of the women in the comparison group who remained free of blood cancer showed the same pattern.

The researchers then examined data from the UK Biobank and confirmed that people showing evidence of these sweeps faced a substantially greater risk of developing AML.

This finding suggests that somatic sweeps could serve as an important early warning sign. However, conventional genetic testing can miss them because the mutations involved are sometimes incorrectly classified as inherited genetic variations.

Professor Jamie Blundell, who led the research at the University of Cambridge's Early Cancer Institute, explained how the team reconstructed the disease's history.

"Serial blood samples are a fossil record of the blood's evolution. They let us go back in time and reconstruct when each mutation arose and how fast it grew. What surprised us most is how predictable the growth of these clones is. Once a clone is established, its growth rate today tells you where it will be years, even decades, from now.".

He added: "Because the growth is exponential, even modestly slowing a high-risk clone over the decade or more before diagnosis could substantially reduce the chance it becomes leukemia. This opens up strategies we can exploit to prevent these clones ever becoming leukemia.".

Could Leukemia Be Prevented Before It Develops?

The discovery could change how doctors approach a disease that often appears to develop with little warning.

Dr. Caroline Watson, the study's first author and a researcher at the Early Cancer Institute, emphasized the contrast between the sudden impact of a leukemia diagnosis and the decades of biological changes that may precede it.

"As a hematologist, I've seen how suddenly AML can change someone's life. This study shows that the changes leading to AML can build over decades, with the affected cells growing in surprisingly predictable ways.".

Watson is also an Honorary Consultant Haematologist who treats patients at the Cambridge Clonal Haematopoiesis Clinic at Addenbrooke's Hospital. The clinic is the first in Europe dedicated to leukemia prevention and already monitors people whose blood cell mutations place them at increased risk of developing the disease.

Industry observers note that she added: "At our clinic, we already assess and monitor people who carry blood-cell mutations that increase their risk of leukemia. Today's findings give us real hope of improving how we identify which of them are at greatest risk and point to a window in which prevention could one day be possible.".

Years of Blood Samples Unlock Latest Cancer Clues.

A major reason the researchers could reconstruct leukemia's development was the availability of blood samples collected repeatedly from the same individuals over many years.

Professor Usha Menon of the UCL Institute of Clinical Trials and Methodology, who led the original UKCTOCS project, highlighted the unexpected scientific value of those samples.

In a recent development, "While UKCTOCS was designed to assess ovarian cancer screening, a key outcome was the establishment of a unique bioresource of serial serum samples. This resource has provided unprecedented opportunities to study how cancers develop over time and to discover and validate biomarkers for earlier detection. We owe an enormous debt of gratitude to the participants whose willingness to contribute their samples and data over many years made this possible. Their generosity is the foundation of this achievement.".

The women who developed AML received their diagnoses between ages 53 and 83. Because the researchers did not have blood samples taken at the time of diagnosis, they could not directly examine the final stage of the disease's development in those patients.

The findings also showed that not every case followed the same extended timeline of detectable changes. In approximately one in five cases, growing populations of mutated blood cells became detectable only one to two years before diagnosis. This suggests that some patients may have a much shorter opportunity for early intervention.

A Upcoming Path Toward Preventing Leukemia.

Despite these limitations, the results offer an encouraging possibility: leukemia risk might be reduced by intervening long before the disease develops.

According to the researchers' mathematical models, even a modest reduction in the growth of high-risk blood cell clones could have a substantial effect over time. Because these cells multiply exponentially, slowing their expansion across the ten or more years between a second cancer-driving mutation and diagnosis could significantly reduce the likelihood that they eventually progress to leukemia.

This raises the prospect of preventive treatments designed to restrain dangerous cell populations rather than waiting until they have developed into cancer.

The next challenge is determining whether such an approach can be used safely and effectively in people identified as having an elevated risk of AML. Although the research provides a promising framework for earlier detection and prevention, clinical studies will be needed to establish whether slowing these abnormal cells actually prevents leukemia in humans.

The research was primarily supported by UK Research & Innovation and Cancer Research UK.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There's a term in science, carcinisation, which is the fascinating evolutionary oddity that sees so many different species end up evolving into crab-like beings. Now, in Everything is Crab, you can too! As this evolutionary, Spore-like roguelike hits iOS and Android!

In a recent development, everything is Crab sees you step into the amorphous shoes of Darwin, a 'blue blob of infinite potential'. From humble evolutionary beginnings, you'll guide Darwin to consume other creatures, growing larger as you might expect from something of this genre. But you won't just get bigger; you'll also gain different attributes from your unfortunate evolutionary victims!

According to recent reports, and no matter how you want to approach your struggle for survival, Everything is Crab gives you a huge variety of options. Whether it's overwhelming them with strength, scavenging the remains littered around each level or actually socialising with and befriending them!

There's plenty there to play, and if you want to, you can give it a go entirely for free. Everything is Crab offers a try-before-you-buy approach, letting you sample what it has to offer with an optional purchase to unlock the full game. Not a bad way to see how evolution works, eh?

Sources indicate that the roguelike has become an increasingly popular genre on virtually every platform. So, if you're looking to sample it for yourself, there's nothing better than the equally popular bullet heaven genre. So why not take a gander at our list of the best mobile games like Vampire Survivors for some of our choice picks?

Download now! Everything is Crab.

#109461. Vampire Therapist review - “The problems of unlife aren't so black and white.”

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1264 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Pocketgamer ↗ Open Full Page

Vampire Therapist review - “The problems of unlife aren't so black and white.”

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1264 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pocketgamer

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that for over a century now, the vampire has fascinated humanity.
  • Industry observers note that in Vampire Therapist, you play undead cowboy Samuel Walls, who is invited to Germany by the three-thousand-year-old Andromachos.
  • Vampire Therapist is a visual novel with puzzle elements where, as Walls, your job is to - surprise, surprise - provide psychological aid to your undead kin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for over a century now, the vampire has fascinated humanity. From books to films, television and yes, even video games, the enigma of an undead bloodsucker that nonetheless has the wisdom of the ages is a contradiction we all seek to understand. Vampire Therapist isn’t concerned with tragic backstories or merciless sadism but with how to move past them.

Industry observers note that in Vampire Therapist, you play undead cowboy Samuel Walls, who is invited to Germany by the three-thousand-year-old Andromachos. For some devious scheme? No, but to help other people. Vampires, that is. Because, as Samuel Walls, you are the one and only Vampire Therapist. And God help you, because these bloodsuckers have some problems.

How can I help you tonight? Vampire Therapist is a visual novel with puzzle elements where, as Walls, your job is to - surprise, surprise - provide psychological aid to your undead kin. To do so, you listen to their problems and aim to catch them in mental contradictions which hold them back from improving or seeing reality.

It can seem a little gamified, but there is definitely a fascinating deductive element to catching your client doing things like Labeling or Disqualifying the Positive, all of which seem to be real therapy terms, but which are explained in a digestible format. The focus is not on catching out your clients, but on taking advantage of these contradictions to show them where they can manage their problems.

Recent findings suggest that you’ll also get to make occasional decisions on what to say or do, which can shift the story in different directions. The focus is mainly on the psychological element, and that in itself is enough to carry the whole game. In fact, I was a little miffed when it got interrupted by a blood-drinking minigame, not least because it was a little janky in the build which I played.

It has been revealed that whenever you have an issue, you can look back at your notes to study them for references to your client’s case files, as well as Sam’s notes that point to the issues they have. You can also look up definitions of the psychological contradictions, including some handy examples. Admittedly, I missed these on my playthrough, but they are there if you’re the journal-reading type, and Andromachos will be on hand to guide you through initial sessions anyway. The Looks and Sound of Death In visual terms, Vampire Therapist is your typical visual novel. You have character sprites with occasional shifts in pose and expression, while vivid backgrounds show which scene you’re in. The art style is a decent middle ground between realistic and stylised, meaning even the more stereotypical vampires, such as the half-century-old Renaissance aristocrat, aren’t boiled down to simple caricatures.

Recent findings suggest that the music in Vampire Therapist is pretty simple, consisting of the main theme and occasional background noises. I did find the track that plays in the vampire club, which your patron Andromachos uses as his base of operations, a little repetitive, which can be an problem since you revisit it pretty frequently.

Industry observers note that the voice acting, however, is undoubtedly a standout. Naturally, Matthew Mercer provides his vocal talent as incidental character Reinhard, and also appears later on in the full game. But Cyrus Nemati is a standout as Sam Walls, who provides cosy mix of stereotypical gravely cowboy and surprisingly self-aware, world-wise wanderer. What’s the story, morning glory? The actual narrative of Vampire Therapist is pretty engaging, and what we find out about Sam Walls, Andromachos and your clients such as Doctor Drayne (yes, really) and Isabella d’Este paints a fascinating picture of vampiric history. There are definitely shades of Underworld and Vampire: The Masquerade, but Vampire Therapist stays on the lighter side of things.

The motivations and backstory for your clients also manage to quite elegantly marry typical vampiric tropes with more realistic psychological conditions. Doctor Drayne struggles with addiction, only it’s to an experimental plasma he’s been making at his pharmaceutical manufacturer as part of a synthetic blood substitute.

The Contessa d’Este, meanwhile, is a literal Renaissance woman who struggles with depression and anger at the world, because after funding the great arts in her heyday, seeing Space Wars: Rise of Spacewalker (no prize for what that’s parodying) made her think all her efforts to enlighten humanity were for nought.

Recent findings suggest that about the only glitch I had is that Vampire Therapist, for what I played at least, seems to sidestep some more pressing complications and leaves a lot of questions unanswered about character motivations. Drayne, for example, is mostly concerned that his addiction to the experimental plasma is affecting his workaholic lifestyle, but the fact he has no memory of what happens when he consumes the substance isn’t given any attention at all.

Admittedly, it’d be a bit awkward to delve into Andromachos’ backstory as the Terror of the Mediterranean, and it might well be something brought up in latter parts of the story. Still, it can feel as though there are some elements that should be explored further, especially as we do get a lot of detail about Sam Walls’ path to redemption even in the first part of Vampire Therapist. What’s been biting at you this evening? Vampire Therapist doesn’t have much in the way of issues, as I see it. It’s a solid visual novel with an original premise, some intriguing puzzle gameplay and a genuinely fascinating, intriguing approach to explaining concepts of mental health and therapy that I found quite informative.

The only problem is that it does presume a lot about the player and how they want Sam Walls to act. Especially considering one early section has Walls nibbling (consensually) on some goth necks in a very sensually implied manner. It’s not as though you’re not warned that it delves into mature topics, but if you’re like me and couldn’t stand the romance in something like Baldur’s Gate 3 it can still feel a bit awkward.

Recent findings suggest that but those are small potatoes, and my earlier mention of stuff I think the story could have done better is only evidence of how much I was paying attention to, and absorbing, the world and its characters, which I think is the highest praise you can give anything narrative-based. It’s lightweight, narrow in scale and perfect for relaxing while offering something of a challenge as you learn more about your clients and try to help them ground themselves and, if not resolve, then at least manage their problems. Let’s put a stake in this What I really liked about Vampire Therapist was how it connected the issues faced by immortals to real-world mental problems without seeming hokey. It’s not just that the Contessa is feeling depressed; it’s that seeing the world go from the Mona Lisa to Rise of Skywalker has seemingly given her concrete evidence that her years of patronage to the fine arts were worthless.

This makes Vampire Therapist feel worthwhile for fans of vampire fiction, as well as those just looking for a fascinating story. Add to that the intriguing explanations of therapy terms, psychological distortions and explorations of the (in)human condition, and ironically it feels as though a game about vampires helps to demystify the idea.

If you’re looking for a solid visual novel with a bit of meat on its bones, and some great art and audio that elevates what rather bashfully calls itself a low-budget indie, then Vampire Therapist is a must-play!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A major research review led by Curtin University has found that people with type 2 diabetes face a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease.
  • Sources indicate that researchers analyzed data from 40 studies in a systematic review and meta-analysis.
  • A separate analysis found that people with type 2 diabetes had a 53 percent higher adjusted relative risk of developing Alzheimer's compared with those without the condition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A major research review led by Curtin University has found that people with type 2 diabetes face a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. The findings provide a clearer picture of the connection between diabetes and Alzheimer's, including how much the risk increases and how frequently fresh cases occur.

Sources indicate that researchers analyzed data from 40 studies in a systematic review and meta-analysis. They estimated that for every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes, approximately 4.7 would develop Alzheimer's disease over the course of one year.

A separate analysis found that people with type 2 diabetes had a 53 percent higher adjusted relative risk of developing Alzheimer's compared with those without the condition.

Understanding the Link Between Diabetes and Alzheimer's.

Sources indicate that study author Dr. Emmanuel Adewuyi, an NHMRC Investigator Fellow at the Curtin School of Population Health, explained that the findings offer a more precise understanding of Alzheimer's risk among people with type 2 diabetes.

In a recent development, unlike previous research reviews that often examined multiple forms of diabetes or dementia together, this analysis concentrated specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease. It also measured how frequently people with diabetes developed Alzheimer's, providing an additional perspective on the connection between the two conditions.

"While many earlier reviews combined different types of diabetes or dementia, this review focused specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease and estimated how often upcoming cases occurred," Dr. Adewuyi stated.

"Relative risk tells us how two groups compare, while incidence tells us how often upcoming cases occur: putting those numbers together gives us a clearer picture of the burden of Alzheimer's disease among people living with type 2 diabetes.".

The study, "Incidence and risk of Alzheimer's disease in individuals with type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis," was published in Alzheimer's Research & Therapy.

Materials provided by Curtin University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Sources indicate that running from December 1st to January 5th, the two headlining announcements for this Go Pass are an encounter with Kyurem and a Timed Incubator. Personally, I'm not a fan of Kyurem. I've never really understood why it feels the need to lean so far forward. Its neck must be incredibly sore. Still, a Timed Incubator is always welcome, especially if you get a lot of steps in.

Industry observers note that however, to get your hands on that, you'll need to buy the Deluxe Go Pass ($7.99 or your local equivalent), which also offers one Super Incubator, extra encounters and other rewards. If that's not for you, alongside Kyurem and its potentially sore neck, there’s Rare Candy XL, Premium Battle Pass, and a Lucky Egg available through the free track.

As always, Milestone bonuses activate when reaching certain Ranks. In the regular Go Pass, Tier 1 gives increased XP when levelling up Friendship and x2 Friendship bonus damage when Raiding. At Tier 2, you’ll be able to open up to 40 Gifts a day, receive 125 Gifts from spinning Stops and get 10 extra Gift slots in your bag. Reaching Tier 3 unlocks x2 Daily Adventure Incense duration, and Tier 4 provides increased Stardust and XP from hatching Eggs.

Meanwhile, having the Deluxe Go Pass bolsters those Tier 2 ranks, raising those totals to 50, 150, and 20, respectively. I must admit, I rarely opt for the Deluxe Go Pass, largely because I'm never sure how much time I can dedicate to Go in a month. A good Legendary can certainly make me go the extra mile, but for me, that's not the case here.

#109455. Breaking: 10 Video Game Rivals I Was Never Actually Mad At

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2399 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dualshockers ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: 10 Video Game Rivals I Was Never Actually Mad At

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2399 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Truth be told, I have a bit of a thing for villains who aren't entirely wrong.
  • I will say that most of these are still very much ultimately in the wrong.
  • Note: There are spoilers for every game on this list, including some very substantial ones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Truth be told, I have a bit of a thing for villains who aren't entirely wrong. Give me an antagonist with a tragic backstory and a motive I can halfway get behind, and I will spend the entire final boss fight feeling a little bit bad about winning it. Some of the games on this list are old, which reveals you how profoundly they impacted me at the time I played them.

I will say that most of these are still very much ultimately in the wrong. It’s usually their methods I have challenges with, ranging from questionable to horrific. I'm not going to pretend otherwise. Nonetheless, I can’t bring myself to be angry at them, because they are somewhat justified in their actions, so let's take a look at ten video game rivals I was never actually mad at.

Note: There are spoilers for every game on this list, including some very substantial ones.

According to recent reports, N's whole philosophy is quite uncomfortable when you really think about it: he wants every Pokémon set free, because he believes they are suffering in the care of their trainers. And I'm not being funny, but he kind of has a point. We have spent 30 years catching animals, keeping them in tiny balls and making them fight each other for badges. The entire anime’s premise is that Pikachu didn’t like being stuck in a Poké Ball!

N is so very intriguing, right from the first encounter. Black and White had already given you two rivals in Cheren and Bianca before you even leave your hometown, and yet here is a third one, with his own battle theme and a design that looks nothing like anyone else's in a Pokémon game. He can also hear what Pokémon are saying, and when he tells you that yours genuinely like you, you believe him.

He reveals himself as the king of Team Plasma on the Ferris wheel in Nimbasa City, and later on, a legendary dragon chooses him without him ever throwing a single Poké Ball. You still beat him, though.

Sources indicate that it then turns out that Ghetsis found him abandoned in the woods as a child, raised him alongside Pokémon that had been hurt by humans and turned him into a puppet king, all so Ghetsis could be the only person in Unova with Pokémon. The poor boy never stood a chance. As someone who will never play a Pokémon game without her starter, I'd like to think I'm one of the good ones, but I do understand his concerns.

Recent findings suggest that kirby: Nightmare in Dream Land is the rare case where the hero causes all the trouble. King Dedede steals the Star Rod from the Fountain of Dreams, breaks it into seven pieces and hands them out to his friends, and suddenly, nobody in Dream Land can dream anymore. Considering this is the same king who once stole all of Dream Land's food, Kirby assumes the worst, and quite frankly, I can't blame him.

Recent findings suggest that the problem is that Kirby doesn't even let him explain. When the two of them meet at the fountain, Kirby refuses to listen to a single word and marches off to collect every piece. As far as we know, Dedede simply stays at the fountain the entire time, keeping an eye on things.

Industry observers note that then Kirby comes back, beats him and puts the Star Rod back in place, whilst Dedede hangs on to his feet and begs him not to. Out comes Nightmare, who Dedede had been keeping sealed away the whole time. Instead of saying "I told you so", he inhales Kirby and spits him into the sky to go and fix it, which is a lot more grace than I would have managed.

Lilith's backstory is a lot more relatable than you'd expect from the daughter of Mephisto. She was created as little more than an extension of her father, grew tired of the Eternal Conflict between Heaven and Hell, and ran off with the angel Inarius to create Sanctuary: a hidden world where renegade angels and demons could live in peace. They had a son, the others had children too, and those children became the Nephalem.

It has been revealed that now, the Nephalem turned out to be far more powerful than their parents, and that made the renegades nervous. Some of them argued that the children would draw the attention of Heaven and Hell and should be destroyed, and Lilith did not take that well: she hunted the renegades down and slaughtered angels and demons alike. A number of Nephalem died along the way, too, and I can’t lie: she kind of loses me here a little.

It has been revealed that subsequently, Inarius couldn't bring himself to kill her, so he banished her to the Void and used the Worldstone to weaken the Nephalem, which meant they eventually developed into what became mankind. I will note that her plans for her children weren't exactly selfless, either, since she always saw them as her own army. Still, the man she created them with was ready to wipe them out, and I can see how that might put someone in a bad mood for a few thousand years.

In a recent development, maruki is the kind of man I'd trust with my problems instantly, which is exactly what makes him so difficult to fight. He joins Shujin Academy as the fresh school counsellor after the Kamoshida scandal, he is incredibly easy to talk to, and he genuinely wants to help. He's also a researcher in cognitive psience, which is never a good sign in Persona 5.

Recent findings suggest that his story starts long before he meets the Phantom Thieves. When his girlfriend Rumi fell into a catatonic state after her parents were killed in a break-in, Maruki awakened a Persona that could rewrite cognition and used it to save her. It worked, but she forgot the trauma and him along with it, and he stepped out of her life so he wouldn't bring any of it back.

From there, his dream grew into a world without grief or suffering, where everyone gets the life they always wanted. The catch is that nobody gets asked: he convinced Sumire that she was her late sister Kasumi, and he'd happily do the same to everyone else. That takes away free will and the chance to grow through hardship, and he crossed that line long before we ever got involved. He isn't after money or power, though, and he truly believes he's helping, which is why his Palace was the one I least wanted to break into.

Sure, Sin is evil and the substantial bad, and thus the villain, but technically, we’re talking about every summoner who ever set out to destroy it. For hundreds of years, summoners travelled across Spira with a guardian or two, learned to call the aeons at every temple along the way and eventually made their way to Zanarkand for the Final Summoning. Once there, they would sacrifice a guardian to finally defeat Sin.

The problem is what happens afterwards. That guardian becomes the Final Aeon, and once Sin is destroyed, Yu Yevon possesses it and turns it into the next Sin. The Calm that everyone celebrates is really just the new Sin being created and slowly gaining its power, and so the whole cycle starts over again.

Industry observers note that so why did they keep doing this for hundreds of years? Well, nobody knew until it was far too late. The sacrifice of the summoner and a guardian was common knowledge, but the fact that the guardian would become one with Sin was not, and summoners only learned the truth once they met Yunalesca in Zanarkand. By that point, you've gathered your aeons, travelled across the entire world and are about to go toe-to-toe with the biggest bad there is. I can't really blame a single one of them for going through with it.

Fou-Lu does not make a great first impression. Within minutes of waking up, he has two soldiers killed for bragging that the Fou Empire could crush dragons, and he looks rather pleased with himself about it. To be fair to him, he has just woken up from a centuries-long nap, and nobody is at their best first thing in the morning.

Recent findings suggest that he is the God Emperor, the other half of Ryu and the founder of the Fou Empire, who went to sleep with a promise that he would take back the throne once he awoke. The current Emperor would rather he didn't. General Yohm hunts him across the country, sets forests on fire and throws monster after monster at him until Fou-Lu crashes into the woods, barely alive.

He wakes up in a little farming village, where a kind woman named Mami takes care of him, and for a while, it's genuinely sweet. Then imperial troops show up, Mami helps him escape, and the Empire fires at him. Before he blacks out, he realises that Mami's life was used to power the weapon. Wanting to wipe out humanity might still be a bit much, but quite frankly, I'd be grumpy too.

Loewe's backstory is incredibly bleak: he grew up in Hamel, a small Erebonian village near the Liberl border, and he was in love with Joshua's older sister, Karin. When the village was massacred to start a war, he lost his family and Karin, and he was right there when it happened. That alone would be enough to send anyone down a dark path.

What really gets me, though, is what happened afterwards: once the war was over, the massacre was quietly covered up, and the official story was that a landslide had destroyed the road to the village. Loewe had no way of seeking justice and nobody to even acknowledge what happened, so he and Joshua made Karin's grave themselves.

Industry observers note that so he joined Ouroboros, became its Enforcer No. II, the Sword Emperor, and set out to make the world face the injustices it would rather sweep under the rug. He is cold and terrifyingly strong whenever he reveals up, but he still looks out for Joshua for Karin's sake. Without spoiling too much, finding out who was really behind Hamel only makes it worse.

In a recent development, I have played Tales of Symphonia more times than I can count, and Mithos gets more tragic with every single playthrough. Long before the game begins, he and his sister Martel were half-elves, hated by humans and elves alike, and driven out of their home because of it. Even so, they went on to end the Ancient Kharlan War together with Kratos and Yuan, and became heroes.

Then Martel was killed, and her dying wish for a world without discrimination turned into something rather sinister in his hands: the Age of Lifeless Beings, where everyone would be the same emotionless being, so that there would be nothing left to discriminate against. Over 4,000 years, that idea only gets worse. By the end, he is mostly fixated on bringing his sister back.

It has been revealed that the game clearly wants you to see him as the villain, but it also makes you understand him, and that is what makes him so well written. Raine and Genis have to hide that they're half-elves to protect her teaching job and his education, and even they can't fully dismiss his points. Tales of Symphonia is quite heavy-handed about discrimination, I will say, but it was pretty profound.

Psaro's motivation is almost sweet, as far as wanting to wipe out humanity goes: he is in love with Rose, an elf who cries ruby tears. Naturally, greedy humans want those tears, not knowing that they break very easily, so Psaro builds her a little tower far away from all of them. Rose, meanwhile, keeps asking him to make peace with humans, which he refuses to do.

He isn't innocent, mind you. Egged on by his advisor Aamon, and after hearing that a human hero is prophesied to defeat him, he starts hunting down young humans, which is how the Hero's village gets destroyed at the start of Chapter 5. When Rose is then killed by humans, he loses it completely and transforms himself into Psaro the Manslayer.

Recent findings suggest that the remakes added a sixth chapter, and that is why he made this list. You find a World Tree flower that can bring someone back from the dead, use it on Rose, and her tears turn Psaro back to normal. It also turns out that Aamon arranged her death to take over monsterkind himself, so Psaro joins your party to deal with him. He even got his own game in 2023, Dragon Quest Monsters: The Dark Prince, which feels like a well-earned redemption arc.

Saturos and Menardi were right, and boy, does that annoy me. For the entire first Golden Sun, they are the villains: they raid Mt. Aleph, steal the Elemental Stars and set off to light the four Elemental Lighthouses, which would release Alchemy back into the world. Alchemy was sealed away because it could destroy everything in the wrong hands, so naturally, you chase them across the continent and stop them.

Then The Lost Age hands you Felix, who has been travelling with them all along, and the whole story flips. Without Alchemy, the world of Weyard is slowly dying, and its edges are crumbling into the void. Their hometown of Prox sits right next to the Mars Lighthouse at the far north of the world, and it is drifting closer to that edge by the day. Menardi's younger sister Karst and her partner Agatio carry on where the first two left off, because their entire village depends on it.

According to recent reports, instead of explaining any of that, they went for sneaky and threatening, and they even kept Felix's family locked up in Prox to make sure he'd cooperate. I do understand why, though: nobody was going to believe two strangers claiming that the world was falling apart, especially when hardly anyone could ever travel far enough to see it. A little more communication would have saved everyone a lot of trouble.

Tech Report: Scientists discover a surprising link between weak bones and faster brain aging

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1148 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than previously understood.
  • The findings, published in Radiology, a journal of the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA), suggest that bone health and brain aging may be more closely connected than scientists once realized.
  • It has been revealed that bone mineral density reflects how much mineral material, including calcium, is present in a given volume of bone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than previously understood. A latest study from Johns Hopkins University found that people with lower bone density in their spine experienced faster cognitive decline and more rapid deterioration of the brain's white matter as they aged.

The findings, published in Radiology, a journal of the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA), suggest that bone health and brain aging may be more closely connected than scientists once realized.

It has been revealed that bone mineral density reflects how much mineral material, including calcium, is present in a given volume of bone. Lower density makes bones more fragile and increases the likelihood of fractures. Although the effects of bone loss on skeletal health are well established, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how declining bone density might relate to changes in the brain.

Using AI to Investigate Bone Density and Brain Health.

To explore this connection, a research team led by Sara Momtazmanesh, M.D., a postdoctoral research fellow in the Department of Radiology and Radiological Sciences at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland, examined existing data from the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA). The analysis included information from participants who had undergone chest CT scans without contrast dye, multiple types of brain MRI examinations, and tests measuring cognitive performance.

The researchers applied a deep learning algorithm developed in the laboratory of Shadpour Demehri, M.D., a Johns Hopkins professor of radiology. The AI system analyzed non-contrast chest CT images from 2,086 MESA participants to determine their initial thoracic vertebral volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD), a measurement of bone density in the spine.

Of those participants, 715 had the required bone density measurements along with brain MRI results and cognitive testing, making them eligible for the final study group.

Industry observers note that the researchers examined the MRI scans for two indicators of changes in the brain's white matter. The first was white matter hyperintensities, areas of abnormal tissue that appear unusually bright on certain MRI images. The second was reduced fractional anisotropy, a measurement that can indicate deterioration in the microscopic organization of white matter. Both types of changes have been associated with cognitive decline and a greater risk of dementia.

Follow-up imaging data were available for 408 participants for white matter hyperintensities and 405 participants for fractional anisotropy, allowing researchers to examine how these brain changes progressed over time.

Lower Bone Density Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline.

The analysis revealed a notable pattern: participants with lower spinal bone density at the beginning of the study tended to experience a faster decline in overall cognitive performance.

According to recent reports, the researchers also identified changes in specific brain regions that are notable for thinking and memory. Lower bone density was associated with greater accumulation of white matter hyperintensities in the corpus callosum, a structure that supports executive function, working memory, and attention.

Another connection emerged in the anterior limb of the internal capsule, a brain region involved in executive function. Participants with lower bone density highlighted a more pronounced decline in fractional anisotropy in this area, suggesting worsening white matter integrity.

According to recent reports, "This study is the first longitudinal secondary analysis linking baseline vertebral bone mineral density to changes in white matter structure, white matter hyperintensity progression and cognition," Dr. Demehri mentioned. "This comprehensive study using both imaging and clinical assessments sends a clear signal that bone density at baseline is associated with both functional and imaging measures of age-related brain degeneration.".

Despite the connection between weaker bones and declining brain health, the researchers emphasized that their findings do not establish that osteoporosis causes dementia.

Instead, bone deterioration and brain degeneration may be consequences of some of the same biological changes that occur with aging.

"This study is not about cause and effect, but rather the observation of a metabolic syndrome that may cause both bone and brain degeneration," Dr. Demehri mentioned. "The co-occurrence observed in the study may reflect shared metabolic drivers of aging, including insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and menopausal change, rather than a direct bone-to-brain effect.".

Industry observers note that these findings raise the possibility that identifying people with reduced bone density could also help recognize those at greater risk of neurological decline. Earlier identification might create opportunities for additional screening and better management of risk factors that affect both skeletal and brain health.

Routine CT Scans Could Reveal Hidden Signs of Brain Aging.

One potentially valuable implication of the research is that doctors may be able to obtain useful information about bone density from CT scans that patients have already received for unrelated medical reasons.

It has been revealed that "Chest CT is done for lung cancer screening, calcium scoring, nodule follow-up, and many other indications," Dr. Momtazmanesh stated. "These scans could provide an opportunistic measurement of bone density from the thoracic spine that is associated with a loss of cognitive function.".

By using AI to analyze existing medical images, researchers may be able to identify patterns of age-related disease that would otherwise go unnoticed. This approach could also help scientists investigate why conditions affecting different parts of the body often develop together.

Sources indicate that dr. Demehri concurred: "Diagnostic images contain an immense amount of data that AI can now synthesize at scale across multiple organ systems. This creates a robust, newly feasible opportunity to interconnect co-existing age-related pathologies that have traditionally been studied in isolation and to identify shared biological pathways and potential common causal mechanisms.".

Recent findings suggest that the study highlights a potentially crucial connection between bone health and cognitive function, while also demonstrating how AI could make routine medical imaging more informative. Although further research is needed to understand the biological mechanisms involved, the findings suggest that measurements taken from the spine may provide valuable clues about changes occurring in the aging brain.

The study, "Deep Learning-derived Bone Mineral Density and Longitudinal White Matter Microstructure and Cognitive Decline: Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis," also included Quincy A. Hathaway, M.D., Ph.D., Michael P. Bancks, Ph.D., M.P.H., David A. Bluemke, M.D., M.S.B., Ph.D., R. Graham Barr, M.D., Dr.P.H., Wendy S. Post, M.D., M.S., Mohamad Habes, Ph.D., Ilya Nasrallah, M.D., Ph.D., Susan R. Heckbert, M.D., Ph.D., R. Nick Bryan, M.D., Ph.D., Jose A. Luchsinger, M.D., M.P.H., Mei Wan, Ph.D., Matthew Budoff, M.D., João A. C. Lima, M.D., M.B.A., Timothy M. Hughes, Ph.D., M.P.H., and Christos Davatzikos, Ph.D., who collaborated with Drs. Demehri and Momtazmanesh.

According to recent reports, materials provided by Radiological Society of North America. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

  • Sources indicate that for the 2027 model year, the TRD Pro adds standard red-painted front tow hooks and an exclusive Hot Honey color, which is available for an extra $695.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Toyota 4Runner’s starting price will clear $45,000 for the first time ever. That comes after the base-level SR5 trim receives a $1220 price increase, bringing the least expensive 4Runner up to $45,085. While every trim has increased in price, the SR5’s rise is the most substantial.

Industry observers note that to help offset the upcharge, the base model now features standard heated front seats. The driver and front passenger seats also get standard eight-way power adjustments. Previously, heated seats were standard on the next-step TRD Sport trim, which started at $50,345 and featured six-way manual buckets. However, if you’re someone who muscles through long, cold winters and enjoys a heated backside, the $1220 price hike might feel like a discount when stacked against last year’s options.

See all results for used cars for sale near 90017.

Sources indicate that for the 2027 model year, the TRD Pro adds standard red-painted front tow hooks and an exclusive Hot Honey color, which is available for an extra $695. The Platinum trim now features standard puddle lamps that project the 4Runner logo on the ground when the front doors are opened. Also, the Black exterior color has been renamed “Inked” on all trim levels. Fancy stuff.

Recent findings suggest that beyond those tweaks, several trims roll into 2027 unchanged. However, prices are up across the board. Most trims have increased by about $200, but the hybrid version of the Platinum sees a steeper climb, costing $490 more than last year. The TRD Sport, TRD Off-Road, and hybrid TRD Off-Road have all increased by $870.

Four-wheel drive still comes standard on most trims, but it’s available for an extra $2000 on the SR5, TRD Sport, TRD Sport Premium, and Limited trims, just like last year. All 4Runners use a 278-hp turbocharged 2.4-liter four-cylinder with an eight-speed automatic transmission, and hybrid models add an electric motor to make 326 horsepower.

Every 4Runner is equipped with Toyota Safety Sense 3.0, which includes a host of driver assists such as lane-departure warning, adaptive cruise control, pedestrian detection, and road-sign assist. The base 2027 4Runner SR5 starts at $45,085, while hybrid models start at $55,945. Upcoming 4Runners are available to order now, with vehicles slated to reach dealerships toward the end of this year.

Battlefield 6's next season will speed up battle pass progression, and make it so Redsec players who don't own the game can actually make progress

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ahead of the start of Battlefield 6’s Season 2 next week, Battlefield Studios has shared some insight into a few of the major goals the developer has with the Season 2 patch.
  • Indeed, the broader goals BF Studios shared with players in a new blog post reflect some of what Labs players already went hands-on with, while others are the result of work on long-standing issues with both the game itself, as well as free-to-play mode Redsec.
  • In a recent development, we know that Season 2 is introducing a big new map to the game, Contaminated, which the developer has been teasing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ahead of the start of Battlefield 6’s Season 2 next week, Battlefield Studios has shared some insight into a few of the major goals the developer has with the Season 2 patch. The game’s second season was delayed in mid-January, and the developer even brought back Battlefield Labs to test out some of the new content and features coming with the new season.

Indeed, the broader goals BF Studios shared with players in a new blog post reflect some of what Labs players already went hands-on with, while others are the result of work on long-standing issues with both the game itself, as well as free-to-play mode Redsec.

In a recent development, we know that Season 2 is introducing a big new map to the game, Contaminated, which the developer has been teasing. The map will indeed arrive in the first part of the season, and it’s going to do so alongside a new LTM that “introduces a new element of tactics.” A second, “high-intensity map” will debut later into the season, alongside another LTM where players battle through an underground base, in darkness.

The real meat of the blog post, however, covers the broader gameplay changes everyone will see once the new season kicks off. There’s a massive focus on player progression, especially when it concerns free-to-play Redsec players.

Challenges are being streamlined yet again, with more broad parameters that don’t require specific modes. Some, like dailies, will also allow for assists to count towards their criteria. Less restrictive challenges are welcome, but even more so is the faster battle pass progression.

According to recent reports, BF Studios is changing the rate at which battle pass Tokens are earned from career XP, and making it so they’re earnable by playing the game normally, and by completing weekly challenges. These changes should also help Redsec players, who will also benefit from faster career and weapon XP earn rates - across both battle royale, and Gauntlet. In general, the career experience should feel more rewarding, especially for earlier ranks.

Weapon balance and recoil are two areas that will continue to evolve in Battlefield 6, it seems, and Season 2 is specifically tackling recoil patterns to make them more consistent when you compensate for them.

Sources indicate that movement is being adjusted with the Season 2 patch, too, though thankfully it’s limited to general feel that touches areas like vaulting, ladder transitions, and acceleration curves. You should also see better continuity and consistency between animations and feel.

According to recent reports, audio is getting a pass with the upcoming patch, especially when it comes to footstep and interaction audio. This also extends to something the developer has been working on improving for a while, and it has to do with how the game decides which audio tracks to prioritise in busy situations.

Tomorrow, the full Battlefield 6 Season 2 trailer will be released, while a more detailed roadmap is expected by the end of this week.

TinyBuild CEO Downplays Threats of AI Game-Cloning

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As part of the ever-growing ingress of AI slop into the gaming industry, a fresh threat has recently arisen in the form of AI game-cloning.
  • According to recent reports, developers are taking this threat very seriously.
  • There’s even been rumors that the PC release of Grand Theft Auto 6 could be expedited just to get ahead of the proverbial slop factory that’s already churning out identical open-world crime sandbox games.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As part of the ever-growing ingress of AI slop into the gaming industry, a fresh threat has recently arisen in the form of AI game-cloning. In a nutshell, a user feeds footage and descriptions of a game into their toaster of choice, as well as more specific data like coding cribbed from released demos, and instructs it to make effectively the same game. The infamous recent example of this was Needle in a Haystack Simulator, a small indie game that, following its announcement, received a deluge of AI-made knock-offs that flooded the Steam store.

According to recent reports, developers are taking this threat very seriously. During the most recent Steam Next Fest, which was already plagued by AI slop, several indie devs decided against releasing demos out of concern that bad actors would churn out knock-offs before they could release their actual games. Some developers have admitted to receiving anonymous extortion threats, saying that if a ransom isn’t paid, the crooks will release an AI knock-off of their game before they can release the real one.

There’s even been rumors that the PC release of Grand Theft Auto 6 could be expedited just to get ahead of the proverbial slop factory that’s already churning out identical open-world crime sandbox games.

Obviously, this is a substantial problem, and it’s only going to get worse as AI gets smarter, but at least according to game publisher tinyBuild’s CEO Alex Nichiporchik, developers should not be afraid of these malicious duplicates. As he explained in an interview with Gamesindustry.biz, AI may be able to imitate a game’s basic aesthetics, but game feel is another matter.

As Nichiporchik points out, while AI-made knock-offs of existing or confirmed games may have some superficial similarities, such as setting, basic game concepts, or story beats, those elements are only part of what makes a particular game a unique experience. In fact, it’s the “experience” itself that serves as the primary differentiator, and despite its best efforts, AI can’t do much in that department.

It has been revealed that “There's a reason that every kind of AI slop game feels the same," he explained. "It's because when you try to make something from zero, AI will multiply your skills, and zero times a thousand is still zero.”.

There's a reason that every kind of AI slop game feels the same.

Nichiporchik went on to say that, rather than being afraid of having their ideas stolen, developers should consider what they can do to make their games more difficult to duplicate, primarily in how the game handles and in its core gameplay loop.

Recent findings suggest that as Nichiporchik himself puts it, you could have an entire army of designers and researchers trying to completely duplicate something popular, but it just won’t have that same distinctive zing as the real thing, authentically brought to life by its original creators. It’s not unlike the number of bodies games like Fortnite or Grand Theft Auto have left in their wake as other studios try unsuccessfully to ape their formulas.

“As long as you have great game feel and a great game loop, I think you're going to be OK,” Nichiporchik assured.

According to recent reports, despite his assurances, Nichiporchik admitted that these AI-made games, not unlike fast food, are ubiquitous and rather obnoxious. Part of the problem is that AI knock-offs are basically trying to capitalize on the hype generated by a game’s announcement, as well as promotion like trailers or demos, stealing attention away from the genuine article or even fooling players not in the know into buying the wrong product.

Nichiporchik’s suggestion for this is to narrow the gap between announcement and release. While the standard strategy is to give the hype thrusters time to warm up and let the game accumulate wishlists and word-of-mouth, playing things close to the vest with a faster turnaround seems to work just as well.

It has been revealed that as Nichiporchik explained, the most recent game published by tinyBuild, Probably Stolen - Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim, was announcement-ready as early as May, but tinyBuild and Questing Goose Studio decided to wait until August to announce, then release in October instead. That game’s done gangbusters despite somewhat repetitive gameplay, so it seems like the strategy worked out, and without giving bad actors nearly as much time to try to copy their notes.
